added 7 commits
  • d5e64907...a1659aa1 - 6 commits from branch wireshark:master
  • 6152f579 - expert_remaining, unsigned offsets, ...ret_uint
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/23101/diffs?diff_id=1617008930&start_sha=d5e64907e255e07267ce5765b76215de64b9828e)

I see that 'len' is already uint32_t here - would it be more natural for it to be uint8_t?  I am planning to add something like proto_tree_add_item_ret_uint8() and proto_tree_add_item_ret_uint16() fairly soon for cases where widening to uint32_t (or casting back to smaller type) would be unnatural.
Why would the wider type mather? I think I chose uint32 to avoid multiple functions for basically the same thing.

Sometimes if it is involved in arithmetic with constants, the compiler may warn about potential overflow.  Also, if you need to pass he value into a function, it might be clearer if the type matched the width of the protocol field.  I notice that in lots of case where people fetch one byte, they'll do it into a uint8_t, whereas proto_tree_add_item_ret_uint() wants a uint32_t (or an ugly cast).
If in this case you preferred to store it in a 32-bit variable, this is obviously fine.

Still not sure why we would like to have all the 8 16 24 32 48 64 bits versions of storing the retrived value. Like in this case it's used to add to offset(unsigned) and as the length parameter also unsigned.
